item.title: Slow Medicine in a Fast System
item.description:
Integrative Medicine

Slow Medicine in a Fast System

What happens when psychiatry ignores the origins of symptoms.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • Modern psychiatry treats the body as a machine to be fixed, but healing requires the patience of a gardener.
  • Doctors found a brain infection but siloed it. My psychiatric distress was treated separately.
  • The people closest to a patient hold longitudinal knowledge the clinical system is not designed to integrate.
  • When psychiatric treatment fails repeatedly, clinicians need time and permission to reopen the diagnosis.
Source: Sandie Clarke/Unsplash

In Slow Medicine, physician Victoria Sweet delineates two ways of making sense of the human body. Modern medicine views it as a machine. You just need to find the broken part, repair or replace it, and the job is done. But Sweet, inspired by the writings of the 12th-century abbess Hildegard of Bingen, resuscitates an older model: the body as a garden to be cultivated. When a garden falls out of balance, the gardener's job is to remove whatever is obstructing growth and provide the organism succor—sunlight, water, nutrients, time. Only then can the intrinsic healing power of what Hildegard called viriditas do its work, reaching a self-regulating level of what we call homeostasis today.

Sweet calls this approach slow medicine. It is not a disavowal of fast medicine, which is necessary in an emergency. But it is an antidote for a different kind of poison: the complex case where a clinician's focus on what needs immediate treatment overshadows the demand for a deeper investigation into the origins of pain. The practice of medicine requires different speeds for different kinds of suffering.

Two Silos, Two Epistemologies

I know this because complexity is what my own illness warranted, and what it never received.

In December 2016, in the wake of my fourth suicide attempt in nine weeks, I lay in a medically induced coma in a hospital ICU. The intensivist directed a question to my family that no psychiatrist ever asked: Tell me about Patrick. What is he like as a person? She asked because she was weighing whether to withdraw life-sustaining treatment. My mother sobbed. For 10 minutes, my family recounted who I had been before the collapse. The question that should have opened every psychiatric encounter arose only when my life was ending.

Days later, after I was extubated, a medical fellow greeted my mother with news: a blood test had come back positive for syphilis. A lumbar puncture confirmed neurosyphilis—a spirochete infection that had inflamed the regions of the brain that govern mood regulation, impulse control, and perception. Syphilis has long been called the Great Imitator; it can mimic psychiatric illness with uncanny fidelity. The fellow was excited. This could be the answer, he said.

But the psychiatry team did not share his enthusiasm. What followed was not an integration but a partition. While the internists initiated IV penicillin, the psychiatrists continued treating my depression and anxiety as a distinct problem. Two silos with two consult notes. No one considered whether the neurosyphilis might be intersecting with an underlying bipolar vulnerability. No one connected the manic episode that had preceded the suicidal months of depression to the tiny syphilis bugs now confirmed in my cerebrospinal fluid.

The correct diagnosis—bipolar I disorder—would not arrive for four more years. Four years without lithium. Four years in which every surge of confidence was read as willpower and every crash as moral failure. My cousin texted me suggesting bipolar disorder less than a month after the hospitalization. She intuited what the professionals could not articulate. But familial prophecy without institutional authority lacks a white coat, a prescription pad, and a billing code.

This is the gap that slow medicine seeks to close. My case is an extreme illustration of a more general problem: symptom management can become its own blinding epistemology. Clinicians can grow so adept at treating symptoms that they stop asking about their source. In Let Me Heal, medical historian Kenneth Ludmerer observes how it became easier for psychiatrists to give patients drugs than to engage in counseling and psychotherapy—even with patients who stood to benefit most from such non-pharmacological treatment. Participants at a Harvard conference captured the existential cost: doctors' struggle to spend quality time with patients has distorted the profession's understanding of what medicine is even about.

Source: Sandjaya/Pixabay

The Question Before the Answer

My mother was the only one asking the right question throughout those years: Where is this suffering coming from? She had no answer. But she had the right question. And in slow medicine, the right question marks the beginning of quality care.

While a master's-prepared nurse and bioethicist, she was not trained in mental health. But she had watched me disintegrate over years and possessed a type of knowledge that was longitudinal and intimate. She could see the pattern of decomposition because she was not seeing me in quarter-hour increments. A gardener does not tend to a plant once, assess its appearance, and never return. Gardening draws on memory, observation, and context—what a 15-minute appointment all too often ignores.

When I was finally diagnosed with bipolar I, the diagnosis was made by a system that was under-resourced and overstretched by a pandemic. My mother had spent years accumulating a meticulous archive of my disturbing behavior—incidents, emails, intelligence from friends and family who monitored my social media; however, none of it was visible to the treating psychiatrist, who was working from what I alone disclosed during a manic episode. And because my illness involved anosognosia—damage to the brain that prevented me from recognizing I was sick—what I chose to disclose was unreliable from the outset. My mother's knowledge was key collateral history that should have been part of the treatment plan. But the system had no room for it.

To be clear, many of the clinicians who provided me with care were competent and conscientious. But they were part of a deficient culture and practice of fast medicine that could not hold the full ecology of my suffering—the observations my mother could have given the doctors that no one had made the time to hear.

What would slow medicine look like in psychiatry? It would look like time. Time to take a full history—a life story, not just a symptom inventory, one that involved the family. It would look like time to think creatively about how a confirmed brain infection historically known to copy the appearance of psychiatric illness might connect to the psychiatric illness actually presenting in front of them. And it would look like diagnostic humility: a willingness to think outside the pharmacology toolbox when treatment repeatedly fails, when symptoms evolve, and when the story does not cohere. The question was never whether the first diagnosis was foolish, but whether anyone would look for the origin of my suffering. Time to wonder.

Slow medicine cannot promise an answer. It can only promise the conditions under which the right question might finally be asked—the way a gardener kneels beside what is failing and, before reaching for any tool, tries to understand what is happening underneath the soil.

item.title: Is Football Losing Ground Among Young Athletes?
item.description:
Traumatic Brain Injury

Is Football Losing Ground Among Young Athletes?

Brain health concerns are driving a cultural change in youth athletics.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • Participation in youth tackle football is declining as parents seek safer alternative sports.
  • Flag football offers 19 times fewer head impacts than tackle football, drawing increased parental interest.
  • Modern youth sports trends favor fluid, less specialized, co-ed games like basketball, lacrosse, and soccer.

In America, each fall, football dominates our national psyche. The game outdraws news of an ongoing war, worsening inflation, climate degradation, and reporting on natural disasters. Political crises, economic uncertainty, waning faith in government and other key institutions, efforts to immunize against disease, and other hot-button concerns trail interest in our favorite form of entertainment—football.

Football is so thrilling, so insistently promoted on television and social media, and so geared to producing stellar athletes and their memorable performances that it attracts 150 million American fans.

Football has its feeder systems that sustain interest. These start with grade school teams and skills-building, bolstering individual bravery and teaching lessons about the value of teamwork. Football enlivens family life and supports social life, generating loyalty. The game yields up its local heroes in small towns where civic life centers on Friday night football. Colleges build their reputation on football. We easily forget which university employs this year’s Nobel Prize winner, but we’ll remember that star quarterback.

The game saturates our emotions, focuses our attention, colors our feelings about success and failure, bolsters our belief in meritocracy, makes us proud, lionizes the underdog, and draws us together—rising above (or obscuring) issues of race or class that elsewhere so divide us. Football has a lot going for it.

Week by week, local journalists and podcasters amp up enthusiasm. The Monday following, news outlets feature highlights—the last-minute game-winning touchdowns, the near-superhuman receptions, the 60-yard science-fiction-like field goals, the heroic goal-line stands, unexpected game-changing interceptions and fumbles that we so keenly count on, the punishing tackles that look so good on video that millions re-share the footage, and those injuries that alter a team’s playoff prospects.

The Cheeky Question: Will Football Survive Brain Damage?

There is a lot to be said for football, and there is a lot to be said about it. In a recent “Play in Mind” post, I followed the apparently audacious question that journalist and ethicist Chuck Klosterman asked about the future of football: Will the game be around three generations from now? Will it, in time, follow the diminishing fortunes of fencing, horse racing, boxing, and—so the trend looks—baseball, too? Will football become a regional niche?

How long can the seasonal riveting hoopla, fabulous financial inducements, and the sex appeal of celebrity even for high-schoolers persist in the face of mounting evidence of cumulative brain injury? Players, with linemen at the forefront, sustain micro-concussions on every play. And these add up. The longer and harder one plays, the worse the effects.

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy, CTE, is the looming ethical, economic, and legal elephant loitering in the room for the future of football. Klosterman asks pointedly, “Why has society coalesced around a sport that wrecks people's brains?”

Why, indeed?

The most alarming study, released a month ago, determined that of those retired players who died between 2016 and 2021 who had arranged for post-mortem examination, an alarming 91.4 percent tested positive for CTE. Note: CTE sufferers experience impaired balance, memory loss and confusion, and a range of “executive dysfunction” which includes difficulty in planning and in concentrating, mood swings and explosive outbursts, anxiety, depression and apathy, and suicidal rumination. This is a sobering list.

Popularity Does Not Ensure Permanence

Football is so deeply anchored in our present that it's hard to imagine it won’t continue to thrive. As families make individual decisions about withholding permission for their kids to play football, though, we are already seeing massive, collective shifts that may starve football of new recruits. Suburbia is leading the change.

article continues after advertisement

In 2021, a survey of private high school sports participation showed that, among male athletes, soccer has edged out tackle football, 29 to 25 percent. At charter schools where parents are more highly engaged, the trend is even more precipitous. At these schools, almost six in 10 students aspire to play basketball. More than a third want to be soccer players. Put together, volleyball and track and field outpace football. The trend arrow points downward. In the decade after 2016, tackle football participation declined between 7 and 12 percent.

The gap between the popularity of the spectator sport and the participatory sport has begun to widen.

So, What’s Next?

A collection of alternatives waits in the wings. Flag football rises in popularity. The game trains the body, the mind, and the social sense much as tackle football does. Crucially, flag football entails more running and less crunching than tackle football. With collisions minimized, as the Centers for Disease Control estimates, flag-football players experience 19 times fewer high-intensity head impacts. Parents have begun to notice.

Two budding lacrosse players gear up for the big game.
Source: Photo courtesy Scott G. Eberle, use only with permission, (2026).

Another fast-paced and increasingly popular physical game, lacrosse, holds a key distinction: It is a contact sport but not a collision sport. In Canada, where lacrosse rivals hockey as a national game, data indicates that football players suffer 10 times more injuries than lacrosse players. Game rules reserve their severest penalties for head-to-head contact, including ejection from the contest.

Wrestling, while surely a kind of individual combat, trains strength, toughness, and self-reliance; it also tests cleverness and alertness while minimizing collision. Wrestlers won’t avoid bumps, scrapes, strains, and sprains. But no wrestler gets blindsided on the mat. Basketball, for its part, entails plenty of shoving and bulldozing on the court, and allows accidental contact. A deliberate elbow to the head, however, gets a basketball player tossed out.

Now nearly 900,000 young men and women in almost equal proportions play soccer, a demanding game of skill, fitness, and cunning. Quick pivots make soccer hard on players’ knees and ankles. But concussion is about 80 percent less likely than in tackle football. The micro-concussions, those impacts that accumulate so tellingly in football, are largely absent. In soccer, goals are few and far between. Keen expectation puts spectators on the edge of their seats.

article continues after advertisement

As Culture Changes, the Games Change

One last observation of a cultural and psychological nature. With its rigid timing, tightly controlled plays, specialized tasks (and bodies), centralized management, and male dominance, football seems to be a 20th-century business.

Three rising sports differ in 21st-century ways. Basketball, lacrosse, and soccer are fluid games that women and men play. Play itself is mostly continual. Positions are less specialized; tasks are more reactive. Coaches outline general strategies rather than dictating specific plays. Players rove the court, the field, and the pitch as play shifts, in real time.

Our 21st-century work rhythms and team play seem to be converging. As much as the neural toll will influence parents’ guidance, these powerful cultural and psychological trends may determine the fate of football.

item.title: 5 Essentials to Cover When Interviewing Gen Z
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

5 Essentials to Cover When Interviewing Gen Z

Navigating young job candidates requires a new approach to hiring.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • Fresh graduates often have little to no job experience and require guidance from the hiring manager.
  • Beyond professional conduct, Gen Z job candidates may need coaching on workplace expectations and demands.
  • A five-step process ensures hiring managers gain insight into a Gen Z candidate's character.

Are you hearing what I’m hearing? Hiring managers are encountering some interesting job candidates these days, and the interview process is… well… stranger than it used to be.

Often, a candidate has never done a job interview before; they don’t understand professional conduct; or sometimes, they’re just young and nervous. A survey from CareerBuilder and Harris Poll of more than 2,500 human resource managers shared the most memorable job candidate mistakes:

  • One job candidate sang her responses to the employer’s questions.
  • Another raised his voice, yelling that the job interview was taking too long.
  • When asked why he wanted the position, one interviewee replied that his “wife wanted him to get a job.”
  • Still another stood up and put her hand on the employer's chest, saying she wanted to connect “heart to heart.”
  • Lastly, one candidate did a virtual interview while in the bathroom… and flushed.

While these accounts seem surreal, let me remind you of the current landscape for Generation Z in the job market. First, they feel empowered. When employers laid off thousands of young staff during the pandemic, Zers now wonder why they should display loyalty when those employers didn’t show any loyalty to them. (Gen Z was among the first to be let go.) Second, they feel needed. They come in choosy about entry-level jobs and won’t take positions earlier generations of young candidates took. In fact, they often interview the employer, not just vice versa.

Call it the “democratization of the workforce.” The ground is more level, and interviews must now uncover characteristics before the recent graduate is hired. Keep in mind—while this isn't bad news, it does require us to be savvier and more investigative in these interviews.

Interview to Discover PERKS

First, beware of terms that Gen Xers and Boomers use that are a turnoff for Gen Z. It doesn’t mean you must cave to cancel culture—it just means you want to dodge biases that put a wall between you; terms that prevent you both from really getting acquainted. Avoid formal jargon and use conversational language.

You’ll also want to figure out who they are before you offer them a job. Hiring managers report Generation Z often enters a job with demands or expectations that past generations would not have expressed in an interview. Because of this high sense of agency they bring, I recommend you use a template I call PERKS. It’s an acronym that enables you to discuss important issues up front and discover who they are.

Once you cover the basic job description, values, and culture, this list offers both you and the candidate a template to share your:

  • Preferences. Ask them about what they prefer to be a reality on the job, such as breaks, PTO, community building, policies, etc. These issues are not dealbreakers; just ones to know before they begin on the team. Ask them if these opinions are indeed preferences and not requirements. This will help you lead them better if they’re hired.

  • Expectations. Ask them what they expect at your workplace. Conflict expands based on the distance between expectations and reality. Unmet expectations frequently come from unspoken expectations. Managers who fail to uncover these may later find disgruntled staff who didn’t voice them upfront. Get them out on the table. They’re stronger than preferences.

  • Requirements. Gen Z frequently voices demands about the conditions of their job, having little employment experience. Sometimes, these demands are only preferences that are best to distinguish early on. If their demands don’t match your culture or values, it’s good to know before you hire them. It’s best to show them the door and avoid wasted time.

  • Keys. Often these issues pop up too late. What are the keys to understanding who they are and how to help them flourish? I’ve heard comments like, “Well, you need to know I’m not a hugger!” Or, “I’m an introvert and don’t do well in social situations.” Job candidates may clarify traits, qualities, or their “love language” to help you grasp what motivates them.

  • Salary. This one is obvious, but as you discover who they are, this is a natural place to discuss compensation requirements or desires. Clearly, this should be an issue they’ve already observed when you posted the job opening, but all too often, an interview becomes a place to discover wants and needs on their part. Clarity is king.

I hear more human resources officers complain about miserable Gen Z job interview experiences than any other. Some say it feels like a cross-cultural interaction. This is partly because parents or colleges did not prepare their students for it. It’s also because Gen Zers bring with them their own terms and vernacular. I encourage you to move from interviewer to investigator to avoid unnecessary surprises.

item.title: How to Tolerate Financial Uncertainty While Investing
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

How to Tolerate Financial Uncertainty While Investing

Financial success isn't just about market knowledge—it's emotional regulation.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional regulation is as vital as financial knowledge for sound investment decisions.
  • Urgency and fear often masquerade as actionable information during market volatility.
  • The illusion of control in finance can be costly and fuel unnecessary stress.

Many of my entrepreneurial clients have recently come to my practice wanting to work on money. The more I’ve sat with them, the more I’ve noticed that making sound financial decisions often requires some of the same skills we try to develop in therapy: strong relationships, patience, self-awareness, emotional regulation, and tolerating uncertainty.

The strongest example of this goes back six years, when COVID was ramping up in late March of 2020, and financial markets were tanking. I remember when my dejected client described the moment he sold everything. He pops in for a therapy tune-up roughly yearly and, despite his progress, still laments how hard it is for him when markets dip; he knows markets tend to recover, but he still couldn't help himself in 2020.

In hindsight, he was referring to emotions and fear much more than money: needing to do something when a feeling becomes unbearable. It is a posture I see in couples struggling to slow down to attune to each other, and trauma survivors struggling with the uncertainty of what may arise during trauma reprocessing. The stock market was where my client's fear most showed up.

I am not a financial advisor. But after spending decades learning about investing, often the hard way, I began noticing that aspects of clinical training explained many of my own and others' financial mistakes and successes potentially better than traditional finance principles did. Here is how I think that translates to your portfolio.

1. Time in the market is partly a distress tolerance skill. The longer we stay invested (such as in index funds like VOO, VT, or VXUS, for example), the better we’ll do in most cases. As Buffett repeatedly said: "The stock market transfers money from the impatient to the patient." Trying to time the market can be seductive, just like an anxious person’s impulse to check their phone one more time or a couple's impulse to have the charged conversation at midnight, utterly exhausted. Contrary to my previous post about the omission bias, sometimes the hardest thing to do is nothing. The longer I’ve invested, the less I think success comes down to knowing some secret about the market and more to what we do when our emotions get overwhelmingly loud.

2. Urgency is an emotion (not information). Herd behavior: The market's dropping, so sell now; a stock is taking off, so buy now. The tricky part is that urgency can feel like insight. A stock is moving, everyone seems to know something you don't, and suddenly doing nothing feels irresponsible. Doing therapy for over 15 years now, I see a version of this continuously: a feeling becomes so strong that it starts to feel like a fact. The fact is that historically, the market has always recovered and moved higher long-term. This doesn't guarantee it'll happen again, but the odds are strong. Making the trade is easy. Sitting with the feeling that you need to make the trade is harder. To me, that is often the real work when it comes to money.

3. Volatility is the emotional price of admission. Morgan Housel describes volatility as a “fee rather than a fine.” A fine punishes a mistake, but a fee exists simply to be able to invest. I think about difficult therapy sessions similarly. One painful, or even bad, session does not mean therapy is failing. Discomfort is not always a signal to change course—in fact, I find it often means we're right on track. Just like exercising or surgery, it (distress tolerance) is often essential to long-term success.

4. The illusion of control can be expensive. Many try to manage anxiety through control. Individual stocks can be psychologically enticing to research, watch, predict, and adjust. If we pay close enough attention, the trap is that we can't control something fundamentally unpredictable. But by the time news reaches us, the market has already priced it in. Hedge funds pay for data feeds that arrive seconds ahead of the public, and by the time a headline breaks, that edge is gone. Index funds like those mentioned above, meanwhile, tend to already hold good companies, so you don't need to find them. At some point, seeking more information becomes more about emotions than utility. You have to accept that you cannot know what happens next, trust the plan you made when you were thinking and planning clearly, and let the market do its thing.

5. Borrowed conviction can become borrowed stress. To me, margin is borrowing confidence from your future self. Borrowed money does not merely magnify potential gains and losses; it can magnify psychological pressure. It is easy to feel patient when the stakes are manageable. It becomes much harder when a market movement threatens money you don’t have. South Korea's recent surge in margin debt and leveraged retail investing shows exactly this pattern (Do, 2026). Before taking on additional risk, it may be worth asking whether the decision is coming from a thoughtful strategy or an inability to tolerate what’s happening and what it brings up in you.

6. Systems can work in your favor. One benefit of automatic investing is that it removes repeated emotional decision-making (401(k) plans often do this well). With dollar-cost averaging, for example, you do not have to decide whether today feels like a good day to invest. Over decades, not even finance pros have tended to time the market successfully (Arnott, 2025; Henriksson, 1984). I do this in therapy: We often plan out and rehearse a client's most adaptive response to the situation that tends to overwhelm them. The EMDR future template (mentally rehearsing a future challenge) is one example. Automatic investing can serve a similar purpose: The decision gets made ahead of time, before the emotions arrive.

7. Your time horizon changes your emotional experience. When we get emotionally flooded (like in number two), the present can dominate our entire field of vision. It's a little like staring at the truck directly in front of you in traffic and forgetting that there is a whole road beyond it. Zooming out does not eliminate discomfort, but it can change our relationship to it. Long-term perspective is not just an investment concept; it's key to mental health and emotion regulation.

8. A healthy portfolio usually should not require constant emotional monitoring. Two people can own the same investment and have completely different psychological experiences. One checks it several times a day and feels every movement. The other rarely looks; same investment but different relationship. If a portfolio has you checking 10 times a day, losing sleep, or feeling panicked every time the market moves, that doesn't automatically mean the investment is wrong.

Conclusion

I find financial mistakes are usually linked to lagging distress tolerance. Good therapists can help you tolerate the overwhelming blend of feelings that can arise while sticking to your sound financial plan.

The goal isn't emotionlessness, but catching urgency, fear, greed, or a perceived need to control before one of them makes a bad decision for you.

Good investing often comes down to avoiding emotional mistakes. Regulate yourself first and get the right support. Then decide what to do with your money.

item.title: Here’s the Number One Thing I Do to Feel Worthy
item.description:
Self-Esteem

Here’s the Number One Thing I Do to Feel Worthy

When hard feelings arise, the Feel, Heal, Do framework can help.

Posted September 16, 2026

A friend cancelled our plans. They were injured. They were okay, but they needed to rest. In that moment, I wanted to feel compassion for them. Of course they should take care of themselves; they’ve been in an accident!

However, if I’m being honest, compassion wasn't the first thing I felt. First, I felt rejected. This was a friendship I had been intentional about cultivating for months, and I craved more reciprocity. I had even asked them to initiate more. Part of me took this cancellation not as a sign of care for themselves, but as rejection of me.

What do we do with these feelings we don’t want to feel? This is a central question that determines our self-worth.

We’ve been taught to push past these kinds of feelings. When our spouse gets a promotion, while we’re languishing, we should not feel spite. When a friend gets pregnant (while we’ve spent years trying), we should not be jealous. When a friend needs to cancel to care for themselves, we should not feel rejected. Suppressing negative emotions is the key to being a good person.

Yet I’ve come to realize that to feel worthy, we must treat our internal world as if it matters—our feelings in particular, and yes, even the ones we’d rather not feel, even our pettiness, rage, annoyance, resentment.

What does this look like? Three steps: Feel, Heal, Do. Instead of trying to push away my feelings of rejection, I could feel them (I feel rejected) and focus on how they show up in my body (a sinking feeling around my heart), heal by telling myself something I need to hear (you are loved!). If necessary, do by asking something from the people in my life (I’d love to support your pregnancy, but it brings up a lot for me since I haven’t been able to have kids. I’m sadly going to have to sit out the baby shower.)

It makes sense why we often opt to ignore our negative emotions instead. We think if we don’t, we’ll become unreasonable or self-absorbed. I need to suppress my annoyance that my friend is five minutes late so I won’t lash out. But it’s the opposite. A meta-analysis including nearly 45,000 people found that the more we endorse certain statements—“I criticize myself for having irrational or inappropriate emotions”—the poorer our mental health.

The more we accept our emotions, even the ones we’d rather not have, the more likely they are to simmer. We can only regulate feelings we are willing to acknowledge. When we accept how we feel, we don’t spend the first 10 minutes with our friend withdrawn, giving clipped answers, because we’re annoyed. The more we allow our feelings, the less they hinder compassion for others.

As I interviewed Dr. Skyler Jackson, a public health professor who is secure-ish (which I advise over becoming secure, so we can always leave room to acknowledge and heal the parts of ourselves that aren’t), he told me he would “run [my] hand over these small things just to see if there’s energy somewhere.”

This was revelatory to me.

I was used to confronting painful feelings when they were obvious, but not to searching for them. Once I did, I noticed myself blotting out these feelings so quickly that they became smudged—like fresh ink from a pen. I couldn’t even make out what they once were. It was clear that a part of me felt threatened by these emotions–ashamed, wrong, bad. It’s been a transformative practice to try to find–and care–for these emotions I’ve spent my life unwilling to feel.

Even the parts of you that you struggle with– your rage, your bitterness, your vengefulness–are parts of you. And, thus, they are precious. As I put it in Worth, “To become truly good, we’ll instead, sometimes be bitter, weak, ungenerous, upset, or desperate because the only way to become anything different is to inhabit the bad things more deeply.”

item.title: Longevity’s Great Experiment
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Longevity’s Great Experiment

The longevity market is booming, but does more medicine make us healthier?

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • Longevity science is increasing the “dose” of medicine applied to healthy people.
  • More testing and clinical attention may find disease earlier, but evidence is evolving.
  • Longevity’s great experiment may be discovering the optimal dose of care.
Source: Image by Mimi from Pixabay.

Longevity certainly seems to be the word of the day. There are longevity clinics, longevity conferences, longevity experts, longevity supplements, and a mind-bending collection of tests and technologies designed to drive both life extension and life expansion.

Of course, there's something very “vital” about the idea. Medicine has traditionally waited for something to go wrong, and longevity flips that model around. The idea is to measure earlier. And look deeper to find risk before it becomes disease. And increasingly, intervene before the problem even arrives—finding “stage zero” disease. And as medicine pushes to earlier and earlier detection, it might find itself adjacent to the elusive goal of prevention.

But there's a basic question hiding underneath all this enthusiasm. How much of what we now call longevity medicine is established medicine?

From Prevention to Prediction

A good deal of longevity medicine is conventional and well established. Things like exercise, maintaining bone and muscle mass, controlling blood pressure and cholesterol, avoiding smoking and managing metabolic disease aren't particularly cutting edge. And they have years of evidence behind them.

Today, longevity medicine has expanded the options. Whole-body MRI, biomarkers, genomic sequencing, disease risk scores, biological age testing and continuous monitoring (think blood sugar and heart rate) are becoming viable options. Then there are interventions including peptides, hormones, various drugs and regenerative approaches such as stem-cell therapies. All of these are entering the dialogue—from the physician’s office to the dining room table.

The issue here is that these don't all carry the same level of proof. Whole-body MRI, for example, can certainly find abnormalities in asymptomatic people, but recent reviews continue to question the routine use, particularly in average-risk populations. The medical literature also continues to advocate for “less hype and more clinical evidence” for longevity interventions.

So, some longevity interventions are being evaluated in real time, or perhaps better said as in our "life" time. Our ability to measure, predict, and even intervene in biological activity that may impact aging may be advancing faster than the evidence that these interventions can extend the length or quality of life.

How Much Medicine Is Enough?

This raises another question that I find particularly interesting. Medicine understands dose-response relationships very well when we're talking about drugs. Take too little and the drug may not work. Increase the dose and the benefit may increase. Eventually the curve can flatten, and at some point, higher does can become toxic.

But what's the dose-response curve for medicine itself?

In this case, the “dose” is the amount of clinical attention directed toward a person over a specific period of time. Conventional medicine is rather low dose, particularly for people who aren't sick or are asymptomatic. A physical, a few office visits, a few recommended (but often avoided) screenings and some blood work might be the typical plan for a healthy person.

A real-world example is Radence, a new company that is tackling longevity with a data-rich and human-touch plan. About six months after launch, the company says it has approximately 50 members. Each receives 120 to 180 hours of multidisciplinary clinical attention per year. This includes physicians, nurse practitioners, pharmacists and genetic counselors. Further, members are assessed across more than 150 biomarkers and receive genomic analysis involving nearly 3,000 genes, along with advanced imaging, wearable data and home monitoring. The average member also receives about five specialist referrals each year.

That's an extraordinary amount of time, data and medicine directed toward someone who may not consider himself or herself sick. And that's precisely what makes it interesting.

Finding More Isn't the Same as Living Longer

Radence isn't simply collecting data. They are using AI to identify key insights, while physicians decide what is clinically meaningful. My sense is that this two-pronged approach is essential given today’s clinical uncertainties.

That may represent an important evolution in longevity medicine. The challenge isn't simply acquiring more biological information. It's deciding what to do to whom. Julie Chen, MD, the company’s chief medical officer, highlights the importance of actionable data.

"The goal isn't simply to generate more data or find more abnormalities. The challenge is determining which signals are clinically meaningful and which warrant action."

But a larger question remains. If we look harder at healthy people, we will certainly find more things. More findings can mean more testing, more specialists and more interventions. Some of those interventions may save lives. Others may simply drive higher clinical utilization and costs.

Longevity's Real Experiment

More doesn't make longevity medicine misguided. In fact, the opposite possibility deserves serious consideration. Traditional healthcare may devote far too little attention to prevention and the biological changes that precede disease. Perhaps much a “higher dose” of clinical attention—both human and technological—will uncover disease or dysfunction early enough to change outcomes.

And that may be longevity's most interesting experiment. It isn't simply whether science can extend human life or whether AI can predict disease years before symptoms appear. We are also beginning to test something interesting about care itself. How much medicine does a healthy human actually need?

The future of longevity may not belong to maximum medicine but to discovering the optimal dose of care itself.

item.title: The Origins of Naturalistic Decision-Making
item.description:
Decision-Making

The Origins of Naturalistic Decision-Making

What gave rise to the NDM movement 40 years ago?

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • Naturalistic Decision-Making (NDM) emerged opportunistically and not as a carefully planned movement.
  • Eight key factors combined to initiate the NDM movement, beginning with simple curiosity.
  • The continued success of the NDM movement is, in many ways, a surprise.
Factors contributing to the origin of NDM
Source: Gary Klein

In late June 2026, we held the 18th Naturalistic Decision-Making (NDM) conference and celebrated the 40th anniversary of the movement. One question came up about how the NDM movement got started. Here are the eight causes that, in my opinion, contributed to the birth of NDM.

First, and perhaps most important, was simple curiosity. The original cohort of NDM researchers wondered how people could make good decisions under time pressure and uncertainty. They didn't worry about doing the right kind of research. They just wanted to satisfy their curiosity.

Second, the government agency primarily responsible for decision research, the Army Research Institute, had been funding the traditional work described by the judgment and decision society. But after several years, they had become frustrated by the products of this research. The results didn't seem to have much benefit to the military community. So they were looking for a fresh approach that they could fund. Judith Orasano set up this new program of a search, relying on guidance from Ken Hammond.

Third, the initial NDM researchers had a great respect for expertise and studied decision-makers who had expertise in fields such as firefighting, military intelligence, and naval operations, relying on researchers such as Robert Hoffman, who was advocating for the importance of expertise.

Fourth, the early NDM researchers tended not to come from university settings and were thus not constrained by the rational analysis models that were so prevalent in academia.

Fifth, in the same vein, the early NDM researchers were able to escape from the laboratory paradigms that dominated the judgment and decision-making research. The early NDM researchers didn't have access to the large population of college sophomores that fueled this research. But in addition, the NDM researchers were skeptical of these laboratory paradigms because they relied on novel and artificial tasks that excluded expertise.

Sixth, the early NDM researchers were able to score some early wins in terms of new valuable models of decision-making; for example, the RAWFS model of uncertainty management, generated by Raanan Lipschitz, and the Recognition-Primed Decision (RPD) model generated by me. As a result, the judgment and decision community could not easily dismiss the NDMers because we had made important discoveries.

Seventh, the NDM community was able to learn from several high-profile tragedies, such as the Three Mile Island nuclear accident and the Vincennes shoot-down incident. Dave Woods and Emilie Roth studied nuclear power plant decision-making, and the Navy created a 10-year research program called TADMUS (Tactical Decision Making Under Stress) to try to understand how the Vincennes shoot-down could have happened.

Eighth, important and lasting bonds of friendship were created among the early cohort of NDM researchers, and this cemented a strong feeling of community within the NDM movement.

To summarize, a number of factors contributed to the emergence of the NDM movement in the late 1980s. In this essay, I have listed the eight factors that seemed most important to me. It was a very exciting time, filled with discoveries. None of the early members of the NDM movement would have predicted that it would still be going strong 40 years later. Looking back, we can appreciate the contributions and imagine a counterfactual—what would have been lost if the NDM movement never happened.

item.title: The Therapeutic Power of "No"
item.description:
Anger

The Therapeutic Power of "No"

Paradoxically, being able to say no is essential to saying yes.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • The capacity to say "No" is essential to the ability to say "Yes."
  • Human will is vitally important to consider in psychology and psychotherapy.
  • Human will can be expressed constructively or destructively and needs to be consciously exercised.
Otto Rank in 1920
Source: Wikimedia Commons

Psychotherapy patients often have problems saying No. Unequivocal No. Unyielding No. Confidently setting firm and consistent limits and maintaining healthy personal boundaries. They frequently fear hurting people's feelings and try to be too kind, caring, or considerate.

Sometimes they suffer from their own co-dependent tendencies, exhibiting an unwillingness to say No to those they love despite their destructive lifestyles. Or they don't feel they have the right to say No to others due to low self-esteem and feelings of guilt and anxiety when they try.

There are benefits of being able to say Yes to life, to relationships, and to oneself, while at the same time cultivating the equal and opposite capacity to assertively, sometimes even aggressively, say No when necessary.

there are times when we need to say No ourselves, to exercise self-discipline, such as when trying to lose weight or quit unhealthy habits. This capacity to constructively express and assert one's will in the world, whether positive or negative and in either way when appropriate, is essential and prerequisite to psychological and spiritual growth and development.


Developmental Roots of Saying No

The word No carries a negative connotation, suggesting stubbornness, willfulness, refusal, dissent, denial, or nothingness. Yet, it is an essential part of our human vocabulary and communication. Human beings start practicing saying No very early in life, beginning around the so-called "terrible twos" (actually at around 18-30 months), during which, developmentally speaking, we are slowly discovering ourselves as separate individuals with our own thoughts, feelings, wants, needs, likes, dislikes, and will. We say No to assert ourselves, set limits, test our power, and learn about how others and the world perceive and respond to us. Saying No is a powerful act of self-assertion and a direct expression of what Alfred Adler (1908) called the "aggression drive," which is present from birth.

Saying No actually begins preverbally during infancy and can, of course, be communicated non-verbally rather than vocally. But when such instinctual self-assertion is consistently met with displeasure, punishment, anger, threats, abuse, and shaming, the child eventually learns that if they want the love, affection, and approval of their parents or caretakers, saying No is not okay. Unacceptable. Wrong. As they later become adolescents and adults, these individuals have difficulty saying No directly to parents, peers, etc., but their will or intention to do so is expressed indirectly in the form of passive-aggressive, defiant, or rebelliousness behavior, social withdrawal, and other types of negative, self-defeating, or destructive acting out. In some cases, this can even lead to the early or prodromal symptoms of psychosis, oppositional defiant disorder, conduct disorder, and other serious psychiatric syndromes during adolescence and early adulthood.

Will, Will Power, and Psychotherapy

Psychotherapist Otto Rank understood that the human will can be communicated either constructively or destructively, positively or negatively, and that when it cannot be expressed productively it manifests destructively. In the latter case, he referred to such an oppositional or negativistic expression as "counter-will." "Will," writes Rank biographer psychiatrist E.J. Lieberman (1985), "represents the life center of the human being, something primal and ultimate. People have trouble acknowledging will personally, just as they had trouble at an earlier time accepting the unconscious and infantile sexuality. . . In psychoanalysis, will was pejoratively called 'resistance.' It was to be met and overcome. Willing has a bad name because it appears as willfulness, obstinacy, protest, insistence, and aggression. . . ."

For some starting psychotherapy, their own will is unknown to them, i.e., unconscious, having been chronically denied, dissociated, and repressed since childhood. Thus, the crucial task of therapy is to render the person's will more conscious to them and help patients to express their own will in the world discerningly, consciously, and as constructively (rather than destructively) as possible. This is no simple matter, since we sometimes do not truly want to consciously know or acknowledge our will. Why? Because if we were ever to admit to ourselves or someone else what we truly want or don't want, we might consequently have to choose it despite the cost--or pay the price for not choosing it.

What is Counter-Will?

Counter-will is an indirect expression of the will of one's entire self, not simply the ego. (See my prior post.) So-called "will power," on the other hand, usually refers solely to what the ego desires. The Rankian concept regarding this neurotic conflict is called counter-will, the negative expression of the person's will, a form of passive-aggressive behavior. Rank's approach, "Will Therapy," sought to cultivate in the patient the capacity to express their will constructively and creatively. But, for Rank, counter-will was not seen as something to be disparaged or discouraged. On the contrary, it was perceived as the person's blocked, dissociated, denied, or habitually repressed vitality, energy, aggression, anger, creativity, and freedom leaking out, albeit typically in negative form. But better that than not at all. In therapy, counter-will teaches us what we really want, and don't want, and helps us to find and fulfill our destiny. Consciously practicing saying No can strengthen one's will and sense of self.

The Heroic Courage to Say No

Saying No can be a negative expression of counter-will, but it can also be seen as the constructive, positive assertion of what Carl Jung called the self. (See my prior post.) Like a muscle, will must be exercised regularly lest it become weak and flaccid. Obviously, saying Yes is also an assertion of one's will in the world. But as with physical exercise, the more resistance there is to the assertion the more empowering the workout. Usually, saying Yes is easier than saying No, because there is generally more resistance, negative consequences, and blowback when we say No. More intense social or interpersonal pressure. People don't like being told No. They frequently find it offensive or insulting. Most family systems punish the naysayer. Society dislikes those who stand up and say No to business as usual or so-called normality and forces the individual to conform and be compliant. To do as we are told and not rock the boat.

This is why it takes so much energy and courage to say No. (Though, for some, saying Yes to certain things such as intimacy, love, or commitment can be equally difficult.) Saying No, as much as saying Yes, reveals who we are, exposes what we truly believe, discloses our ultimate concerns (see my prior post), and displays what we value above all else. Saying No can be and often is an act of extreme heroism and bravery. And when we are unable, unwilling, or refuse to say No as needed, we lose a little of ourselves, our self-respect and integrity is eroded, and our freedom diminished.

Conversely, while consistently saying No to life leads in the long run to nihilism, depression, and possible suicide, saying Yes, despite the inherent human capacity to negate or reject life, is equivalent to what Rank (1929) called the "willing affirmation of the must": the ultimate existential Yes to life and its immutable givens on its own terms, or, as Nietzsche put it, embracing and loving our fate (amor fati).

item.title: 6 Essential Communication Skills You Need to Learn
item.description:
Relationships

6 Essential Communication Skills You Need to Learn

Like driving a car, the key to effective conversations is staying on track.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • The key to good communication is less about the content and more about managing the flow of the conversation.
  • Having a goal, controlling your emotions, monitoring feelings, talking about soft emotions are all important.
  • Like anything else, learning these skills takes practice. Start with casual conversations.
Source: TungArt7 / Pixabay

You may know someone you enjoy talking with simply because of how they handle a conversation. You not only feel listened to, but they also make their points clearly, never get rattled, and keep the conversation on track. Like driving a car, steering a conversation is about skills—skills that good therapists, PR experts, and effective salespeople seem to have and that you can develop, too. Here are six essential skills that create good conversations, as well as the traps to avoid:

1. Have a goal.

Many everyday conversations are back-and-forth, stream-of-consciousness chats with no explicit purpose. But if the conversation has a goal, take a minute or two to decide on it: What do you want the other person to understand, what problem do you need to solve together, and how do you want them to feel when it is all over? Decide before you start talking. Having a goal helps you stay focused and gives the conversation a destination.

Trap: You may have a goal, but you’re not clear about what it is. As a result, the other person may feel like you’re just yapping or complaining, or they may be confused.

2. Use I-statements.

You’ve undoubtedly heard this before. When describing a problem or a feeling, talk about yourself rather than the other person: I’m worried vs. you never do X. Using “you” is like jabbing a finger in the other person’s chest; it can make them defensive, heated, and push back.

Trap: It’s easy to slip into you-statements, especially when the conversation gets heated. Time to return to skill number one and your goal.

3. Talk about soft emotions.

If you’re angry, say so. But for some people, anger is their primary emotion, and they express other, subtler emotions as anger. Anger doesn’t just stir more anger in the other person; they quickly dismiss what you’re saying—there they go again—and never truly understand how you feel. Instead, try expressing softer emotions: concern, worry, fear, confusion. These are easier for others to hear and don’t trigger defensiveness.

Trap: If you’re wired for anger, you need to broaden your emotional range. When you feel angry, ask yourself what else you might be feeling. The first hundred times, you may not know, but over time, you rewire your brain and become more attuned to softer emotions.

4. Track the micro-process.

The car salesman steers you toward a car that isn’t the color you wanted but is considerably cheaper. She says, “Here’s a car in a different color that’s more in your price range.” Then she stops and waits to hear your response: “Great,” or “I hate the color.” Whatever you say, she doesn’t move forward until she knows you are in lockstep with her.

Like the salesperson, you also want to stay in lockstep with the other person, and doing so means tracking the micro-process. This is probably the most difficult of the skills to learn, the equivalent of learning those micro-steering adjustments you eventually learn to keep the car on the road.

Trap: If you don’t notice when the conversation goes off track, or when the other person reacts negatively and is no longer in lockstep with you, conversations can quickly derail.

5. Fix feelings with feelings, not facts.

Once you realize the other person is shutting down, not paying attention, or becoming emotional, the topic—your goal for the conversation—is no longer on the table. The problem in the room is the emotion: the car is veering off the road; it’s time to focus on the emotions.

The natural tendency is to repeat what you said and heap on more information, hoping it will clarify your point. But it never works; the other person’s rational brain is offline, and they can’t process what you’re saying. Instead, the mantra is to fix feelings with feelings, not facts: Stop and ask the other person what just happened—they seem angry or upset. Let them vent. Once they’ve settled and the emotion has drained, circle back to the original goal.

Trap: Instead of lowering the emotional temperature, you both get into the weeds over whose reality is right—the facts. This is like arguing over whose fault it is that the car is off the road, rather than getting the car back on the road.

6. Regulate your emotions.

You can’t control the other person’s reactions, but you can control your own. This is about emotional regulation. If you’re getting worked up, say, “I’m getting upset and need time to cool off. I’m coming back.” I-statements signal responsibility—I’m getting upset vs. you’re acting crazy—and “I’m coming back” lets the other person know you’re not just cutting them off. Often, cutoffs trigger the other person and only intensify their reactions.

Trap: You don’t do any of this, but instead let your emotions flare. You get bogged down in facts, blame the other for upsetting you, and stomp off, only causing more emotional wounds on both sides.

Time to practice

Again, this is about skills. Like learning any skill, it takes practice. When talking to an acquaintance at the grocery store, try focusing on the microprocess. If you want to have a serious conversation with your partner, child, or friend, think ahead to your goal—the point you want to make and the feeling you want to leave them with. Expand your emotional range to include softer emotions. Be deliberate and be aware.

And keep the conversational car on the road.

item.title: The Real Reason High-Achievers Miss Their Year-End Goals
item.description:
Leadership

The Real Reason High-Achievers Miss Their Year-End Goals

The hidden cost of carrying work that should have been delegated months ago.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • High-achievers often delay delegation until the stakes are highest.
  • Q4 often exposes the tasks founders never delegated and the hours they cost all year.
  • Strategic support, not more hours, helps founders hit their targets.
Source: Filip Pesek / Used With Permission

With entrepreneurship on the rise, many founders may be able to relate to having to serve as the business visionary, accountant, sales manager, and executive assistant all at once. As Q4 arrives, many may feel overwhelmed and over-tasked, attempting to get closer and closer to reaching their year-end goals. However, this issue didn’t start in October; it started in January, when the founder decided to take on one more thing themselves, then another, and another.

To explore why this pattern is so common and what changes it, I spoke with Filip Pesek, founder of the European executive assistant agency DonnaPro, who has studied delegation failures from the inside. His experience offers a different perspective on what founders can do to free up their time and attention.

The Psychology of Delegation Resistance

High-achievers share a common cognitive pattern. They are exceptional at solving problems, creating solutions, and driving results. However, many may struggle with letting someone else take over tasks they could handle themselves. One way to explain this is through self-reliance. During their past experiences, it may have been reinforced that if something needs to be done, then they should do it themselves. However, this previously adaptive trait may not be as helpful as they enter entrepreneurship and try to scale their business.

For instance, research shows that constantly switching between different demands takes a mental toll, especially when the work requires different types of focus and decision-making. Over time, this can increase stress, hurt productivity, and make it harder for founders to grow.

Delegating tasks may sound easy in theory; however, in practice it may be challenging. For some high-achievers, delegation can be difficult because doing the work themselves has become part of how they operate. For some high-achievers, letting go is not just about giving someone else a task. It can feel like giving up a piece of what made them successful in the first place.

Why Q4 Exposes What You Refused to Delegate

Q4 has a way of exposing decisions that were made throughout the year. When resources are available, the work that remains on a founder’s plate can reveal a lack of trust or possibly a need for control. In some cases, the problem is not that support is unavailable. The founder who has support available but refuses to let go of work that someone else could handle may find themselves overwhelmed when Q4 gets busy.

Research on delegation suggests that managers often weigh the benefits of handing off work against the perceived loss of control that comes with it. For instance, a 2024 study of 215 managers found that they were less likely to delegate when employee work was harder to monitor. The researchers suggest this may be because delegation can come with a greater sense of losing control. For founders, that can make it harder to let go.

The Cost of Waiting to Delegate

Waiting to delegate isn't just a decision that leads to stress; it can also impact founders financially. For instance, a task that takes 30 minutes may not seem like much; however, there is an opportunity cost when a founder continues to spend their time on work someone else could do. That time could be spent on clients, sales, business development, or other work that requires the founder.

Filip knows this from experience. He hired his first assistant at 19 and spent the next eight years learning what worked, what did not, and where he made mistakes. “I do not believe in overnight breakthroughs,” Filip told me. “Anyone who attributes their success to a single moment is usually simplifying the story, selling something, or lying to themselves. For us, success came from doing many things well, consistently, over a long period of time.” By the time Q4 arrives, the founder may realize how much of their time has gone toward work they could have handed off.

Action Steps

If you recognize this as a roadblock and want to delegate more responsibility, a few questions can help you decide where to start.

  1. Audit your calendar: Identify the tasks that have been there since Q1. Ask yourself, “What benefits would the company gain if I handed some of these tasks to someone else?” Do a cost-benefit analysis to determine where your time is best spent.
  2. Separate “only I can do this” from “I have been doing this myself out of habit”: The gap between those two categories is usually wider than founders expect. If you want to scale, founders need to recognize that they may serve as the biggest bottleneck in their business. Identify where you are holding your business back.
  3. Build delegation into your Q1 plan, not your Q4 stress response: Make this a systemic decision, not an individual one. If it is embedded in your values, business goals, and culture, then delegation becomes part of how the business operates.

Bottom Line

The cost of doing everything yourself may not be obvious until Q4. Founders who want to scale need to recognize what they should have delegated months ago and make the change now rather than waiting for a less busy time. The time is now to stop what has been holding you back from infinite growth.

item.title: 3 Reasons Why Kissing Is Vital for a Successful Relationship
item.description:
Mating

3 Reasons Why Kissing Is Vital for a Successful Relationship

How a kiss leads to positive mate assessment, secure attachment, and arousal.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • Research suggests that kissing performs three essential functions in a successful romantic relationship.
  • Specifically, kissing provides an assessment of attraction, promotes attachment, and sparks arousal.
  • These functions create “affective reciprocity” as partners share enjoyment from kissing each other too.

Why do we make such a big deal out of kissing in romantic relationships? Why does a kiss seem so important for judging chemistry and attraction? Also, why is the exchange of kissing and affection so essential for maintaining long-term relationships and sexual satisfaction, too? Over the years, research has pondered these questions—and provided interesting answers!

Summarizing those answers, kissing appears to serve three main functions: (1) assessing mate compatibility and attraction between partners, (2) attaching those partners to one another emotionally, and (3) arousing each other for sex. Furthermore, when combined, these three functions create what is known as affective reciprocity, which helps strengthen a relationship through shared enjoyment of intimate interactions over time. So, below, we will look at those processes in more detail to support your own dating, mating, and relationship efforts!

Kissing for Assessment, Attachment, and Arousal

Drawing on previous work by Eibl-Eibesfeldt (1972), Wlodarski and Dunbar (2013) noted that romantic kissing occurred in over 90 percent of cultural mating behaviors, which often focused on mate assessment, attachment, and sexual arousal processes. To explore these possible functions of kissing more specifically, the pair surveyed 902 participants about their own kissing and mating behaviors. Their results showed that kissing was particularly important for the initial assessment of mate attraction and later building of attachment.

Specifically, regarding mate assessment, Wlodarski and Dunbar (2013) found that initial kissing (i.e., a first kiss) was more important to high mate value individuals and those most interested in short-term sex (those with a high sociosexual orientation). Somewhat in contrast, regarding attachment formation, the quality and quantity of kissing in an ongoing romantic relationship was most important for bonding among individuals preferring long-term commitments (those with a low sociosexual orientation). Beyond that, women were generally more sensitive than men to the effects of kissing on both initial assessments of attraction and later pair-bonding attachments.

Given those results, it seems being a good kisser is important for creating initial attraction with a romantic partner, especially a high-value mate. As a relationship progresses, continued affection and kissing are vital for bonding with a long-term partner too. Nevertheless, specific partners may place different importance on kissing for attraction or attachment, depending on whether they are more interested in short-term sex or long-term commitment.

Further research by Busby, Hanna-Walker, and Leavitt (2023) also supports the attachment functions of kissing—and highlighted its effects on arousal and sexual satisfaction too. Specifically, they explored the idea that kissing could be both a relationship maintenance behavior (promoting attachment) and part of a sexual repertoire (sparking arousal). To do so, the team surveyed 1,605 participants in long-term relationships about their kissing frequency, sexual experiences, and interpersonal satisfaction.

article continues after advertisement

Results indicated that partners who kissed more frequently were significantly less likely to report anxious or avoidant attachment and more likely to be satisfied with the relationship in general. Additionally, frequent kissing was also related to partners being more aroused, more likely to experience orgasm, and more sexually satisfied overall. Given that, we see the third reason why kissing is vital for relationships. Not only does it create attraction and build attachment, but it also arouses and deepens the sexual connection between partners as well!

Affective Reciprocity and the Kissing Process

Now that we know the importance of kissing for attraction, attachment, and arousal in relationships, we are left with another set of questions… How does someone kiss well? What makes a kiss better or worse?

Katila and Cekaite (2023) answer those questions by explaining that kissing is not a single behavior in isolation; rather, it is a process of intimate interactions over time. Put more specifically, it is a give-and-take exchange, much like dancing, where each partner acts and reacts to one another affectionately (known as affective reciprocity). During that process, they get closer, touch each other more, and ultimately kiss. Furthermore, at each step, they express their joy, interest, and receptivity to each other’s advances, especially non-verbally (e.g., making eye contact, smiling, touching back, etc.).

Most importantly, Katila and Cekaite (2023) share that affective reciprocity occurs when both partners mutually express enthusiasm and enjoyment for the ongoing interaction. As they explain, “For instance, the initiation of a kiss was responded to with enthusiasm, enjoyment expressed via vocalized kissing or kissing melodies was reciprocated, and withdrawing from the kissing trajectory was collaboratively accomplished on a happy note” (Katila & Cekaite, 2023, p. 51). In other words, good kissing partners don’t just go along with a kiss passively or halfheartedly—they happily, readily, and cooperatively participate in the entire kissing process, sharing and enjoying each step at a time.

Conclusion

Together with the above results, the take-away message is that kissing is a step-by-step process, which is important throughout romantic relationships. First, it is part of the human mating process at the beginning (assessing attraction), the middle (building attachment), and the conclusion (sparking arousal). Second, as I detail throughout chapter 11 of my book Attraction Psychology, each intimate episode is also an interactive process of getting close, touching, and kissing as well (Nicholson, 2022). So, much like dancing, you can learn to be a better kisser—and that skill can help make your romantic partner feel more attracted, attached, and aroused by you too!

item.title: Doom Spending and the Emotional Price of Uncertainty
item.description:
Consumer Behavior

Doom Spending and the Emotional Price of Uncertainty

Why we spend during uncertain times.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • Doom spending is often an emotional response to uncertainty rather than a simple failure of self-control.
  • When the future feels unreliable, immediate consumption becomes psychologically more valuable.
  • Shopping can temporarily restore control and repair threatened identities, but the relief rarely lasts.

Why would someone who feels anxious about money respond by spending more of it? Why book an expensive holiday while worrying about job security? Why buy designer shoes when home ownership feels increasingly impossible? Why spend today precisely because tomorrow feels frightening?

This behaviour is increasingly described as “doom spending”: spending despite financial concerns because the future feels too uncertain, unstable, or discouraging to justify continued sacrifice. On the surface, doom spending appears contradictory. If people fear economic insecurity, logic suggests they should save more. Yet consumer behaviour is not guided by financial logic alone. Consumption is emotional, symbolic, and psychological. People do not merely buy products. They buy relief, identity, anticipation, control, and sometimes proof that life can still feel good.

Saving is not simply a financial behaviour. It is a psychological agreement between the present self and the future self. The present self accepts deprivation today because it believes the future self will eventually benefit. Saving for a home, retirement, or financial stability requires people to believe that the future is sufficiently predictable and that present sacrifice will ultimately be rewarded. However, that agreement becomes fragile when the future no longer feels trustworthy.

Research on temporal discounting shows that people tend to value immediate rewards more strongly than delayed ones, even when waiting may produce a better outcome (Frederick, Loewenstein, & O’Donoghue, 2002). When the future feels uncertain, distant rewards can lose even more of their psychological value. A person may begin to think, “If I may never afford a home anyway, what difference will this £200 make?” More than an indulgence, the purchase becomes a certain pleasure exchanged for an uncertain future.

This does not necessarily mean doom spenders are incapable of delaying gratification. They may just no longer believe that gratification delayed will ever arrive. The underlying problem may not be impulsivity but hopelessness: When people stop imagining a future in which their sacrifices will meaningfully improve their lives, the present becomes psychologically dominant.

Economic uncertainty creates powerlessness. Individuals cannot personally control inflation, housing prices, employment markets, or the cost of living, yet these forces shape their choices and threaten their security. Shopping offers a small but immediate reversal of this powerlessness. The consumer can choose the product, select the colour, decide when it will arrive, and experience the satisfaction of completing a decision. The wider world remains unpredictable, but within the shopping environment, the consumer temporarily becomes the decision-maker.

Research on retail therapy supports this explanation. Rick, Pereira, and Burson (2014) found that making purchasing decisions could reduce lingering sadness by restoring a sense of personal control. Some of the emotional benefit came from choosing rather than merely owning the product. This may explain why scrolling, selecting, and ordering can feel soothing during difficult periods. Anxiety says, “Something is wrong, and I cannot control it.” Consumption answers, “Choose this.” The relief is real, but it is usually temporary.

Doom spending may function as compensatory consumption—using products to reduce the gap between how people currently perceive themselves and how they want to see themselves. The Compensatory Consumer Behavior Model proposes that threats to identity and self-worth can motivate consumption intended to repair these psychological discrepancies (Mandel et al., 2017). Someone who feels professionally unsuccessful may desire products associated with achievement. Someone who feels socially excluded may buy goods symbolising belonging. A consumer whose life feels stagnant may purchase travel, fashion, technology, or wellness products connected to transformation.

The product becomes symbolic evidence of a “possible self.” New exercise clothes represent the disciplined person one intends to become. Luxury goods communicate success when success feels uncertain. A holiday booking suggests that life remains exciting rather than stagnant. More than an object, the consumer is purchasing a more reassuring interpretation of who they are. Research has similarly found that feelings of powerlessness can increase the willingness to pay for status-related products, suggesting that acquisition can compensate for threatened power (Rucker & Galinsky, 2008).

The word “doom” is psychologically significant. It captures more than ordinary financial concern; it suggests a broader awareness of social, environmental, political, and existential threats. Mortality-salience research indicates that reminders of death and insecurity may intensify materialistic behaviour. Kasser and Sheldon (2000) found that participants reminded of mortality expressed stronger financial expectations and consumed more resources. When life feels finite, consumption can become a way of asserting existence: “I am here now, and I should enjoy something while I can.”

Digital marketplaces make this response easier to translate into spending. One-click payments, personalised recommendations, disappearing discounts, and buy-now-pay-later services minimise the distance between desire and action. They separate the pleasure of consumption from the discomfort of payment. Research on mental accounting suggests that consumers experience a “pain of paying,” but payment arrangements can weaken the psychological connection between acquiring something and paying for it (Prelec & Loewenstein, 1998). The consumer receives the pleasure now and sends the discomfort to their future self.

Doom spending can become a self-reinforcing cycle. Uncertainty generates anxiety. Anxiety creates a need for comfort or control. Consumption provides temporary relief. The financial consequences then produce guilt, debt, or greater insecurity, creating further anxiety. The behaviour intended to restore control eventually makes the consumer feel less in control.

Shame rarely interrupts this cycle. Telling someone to “be more disciplined” overlooks the psychological function their spending performs. Doom spending is ultimately not about loving products too much. It may be about trusting the future too little. When tomorrow no longer feels capable of rewarding sacrifice, consumers begin demanding their rewards today.
